questions.title: How do multiple overlapping stays and 'vacatur' orders interact in an expedited appeal?
questions.question_body: I am struggling to follow the procedural history in the beginning of the opinion. The court vacates an administrative stay, then vacates a prior stay, but then stays the district court's preliminary injunction 'in their entirety except as specified.' Can someone explain the practical effect of this? If a stay is vacated, does the underlying injunction automatically become active again, or does the 'stay pending final resolution' take precedence?

questions.title: Why does 8 U.S.C. § 1182(f) grant the President such broad deference that the court refuses to conduct a 'searching inquiry' into his justifications?
questions.question_body: The court cites Trump v. Hawaii to say the President's authority under § 1182(f) 'exudes deference' and that he only needs to 'find' that entry is detrimental. Does this mean the court is essentially skipping the 'rational basis' test? If the President's justification is arbitrary or irrational, does the court have any power to review that under this specific statute, or is the 'finding' itself the only thing that matters?

questions.title: How does the court distinguish between the President's power to suspend admissions and the government's duty to provide resettlement services?
questions.question_body: The court seems to split the issue into two parts: (1) the President can legally stop new refugees from coming in under § 1182(f), but (2) the government is violating the APA/statute by stopping services for those already admitted under § 1522. Is there a legal principle that separates 'admissions' (discretionary executive power) from 'domestic resettlement' (mandatory statutory obligation)? Why can't the President's broad discretion over the Refugee Admissions Program encompass the funding of the services for those he admits?

questions.title: When does the word 'shall' in a statute create a mandatory duty versus a conditional requirement?
questions.question_body: The majority argues that § 1522(a) creates a mandatory duty because it uses the word 'shall' regarding resources for employment and English training. However, it is qualified by the phrase 'to the extent of available appropriations.' Does 'to the extent of available appropriations' turn a mandatory 'shall' into a discretionary 'if we have the money'? I'm confused about how a court determines if a duty is mandatory when the funding is technically variable.

questions.title: Does the title of a statute (e.g., 'Authorization') override the use of mandatory language ('shall') within the body of the statute?
questions.question_body: This is the core of Judge Lee's dissent. She argues that because the section title is 'Authorization for programs,' the word 'shall' in the subsections is permissive, not mandatory. Is there a hierarchy in statutory interpretation where the title of a section can override the specific verbs used in the body of the text? If I'm a student, how do I know which one to prioritize when they seem to contradict each other?

questions.title: What is the legal significance of the 'limited carveout' for refugees conditionally approved before January 20, 2025?
questions.question_body: The court mentions a 'limited carveout' for individuals who were 'conditionally approved' before the Executive Order. Does this imply a 'vested right' or a 'procedural due process' issue? If the government has the power to suspend the program, why does the court feel compelled to protect those who were already in the process of being admitted? Is this a matter of equity or a specific statutory protection?
